## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why_b5: The count of 7 people is visible, but four calm *Holding up* verdicts on 6 or 7 reservation agents are never flagged as a small sample, so the page reads firmer than seven answers can carry.
screens.instead: Holding up on 6 to 7 reservation agents, a small group: missed booking calls are frequent and today's cover falls short for all 6 counted, so go on to the commercial page and test whether a revenue director will pay €3,000 for the pilot.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip counts yes answers over 7 people, with my bar marked at 6, and all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: My belief was that booking calls go unanswered, but the card says agents 'had a booking call come in on their shift', which is just my circumstance with the 'not every one gets answered' dropped, so this is not the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards' only points me onward; it doesn't say what this result means for Codyco.
screens.why_b5: The gate asked whether a call came in, which every working agent would say yes to, so no one could say No, yet the card calls my problem's prevalence 'Holding up'; that is a claim the data can't carry, even though the low n is stated.
screens.instead: Ask and state 'In the last 7 days, did a booking call on your shift go unanswered?' so the 7 of 7 says how many agents actually missed a booking.

screens.why_b1: The card says Holding up with the deciding numbers beside it: median 6 days out of 7, 6 of 6 inside my 5 to 7, against a bar of 4 of 6.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts days out of 7 per person, the strip shows 6 counted cells with the marker at 4, and the bar of 4 of 6 (at least 2 in 3) is plain at first look, though the 0 tick sits on an axis where nobody could answer 0.
screens.why_b3: My problem is booking calls that go unanswered after hours, at peak and on holidays, but the line only says a booking call comes in on the shift, which drops the missed part that makes it my problem.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' points me on, but it doesn't tell me what 6 of 6 means for Codyco, for example that the calls come in every shift so the missed share is what to price against.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said ('a small group: a lean, not a call') and Tobias's guess is set apart, but 'Holding up' reads as the problem being frequent when the data shows only that calls arrive, which every reservation desk knows, and the stray 'the most recent time it happened' muddles a 7-day count.
screens.instead: Ask on how many days in the last 7 a booking call went unanswered on my shift, drop 'the most recent time it happened', and have the So line say how often the missed call that Codyco catches happens.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 5 of 6 put it in their two and the bar of 4 of 6, so I know it held and why, though the count line is printed twice.
screens.why_b2: The bar marker and the 6 people are plain, but the caption says bars count picks (12) while the bars add to 10, so I have to stop and work out what is actually counted.
screens.why_b3: The belief line and Answering every call that comes in are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line rightly says top two, not first, but it never tells me what to do next, for instance that Chiara's group, with a call center after six, is the segment where my pitch weakens.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the small group is called a lean, not a call, but the 12-picks caption over bars totalling 10 is a figure the answers do not carry.
screens.instead: Say 6 people picked 10 times (two stopped after one), and add that the one against is a group whose call center already answers after hours, so lead with groups without one.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits directly beside its deciding number, 6 of 6 said today's way falls short against a bar of 4 of 6, and the strip marker at 4 agrees with it.
screens.why_b2: On first look I can see what is counted (the five outcomes, 0 on my working rung and every answer below the line), the base of 6 counted out of 7, and the bar at 4 on the strip.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Current solution and its belief line is word for word the one I checked, with the bar naming my own rung 'Every call answered or called back in minutes'.
screens.why_b4: The So line mostly repeats the tally, and 'judged against this gap on the next study' is a generic pointer that does not tell me which gap to lead with, for example that 4 of 6 lost or never returned most missed calls, which is the case for an AI answering them.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 6 counted, Tobias's guess left out), the line 'a small group: a lean, not a call' tempers the 6 of 6, and nothing is claimed beyond these people.
screens.instead: Ask about my last reservation shift rather than 'your last call' (one call cannot test 'every call'), and in the So line say that 4 of 6 lost most of their missed calls, so that is the loss my AI answering has to recover.

screens.why_b1: The verdict *Holding up* is stated, and *5 of 6 put it in their two · bar 4 of 6* sits beside it, repeated as *Importance held, 5 of 6*, so I know it held and by how much over the bar.
screens.why_b3: The name *Importance* and the belief line match word for word what I checked on the way in, call-coming-in circumstance and all.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do with this: it does not say whether groups whose call center already covers after six are a weaker segment, or whether group emails and channel rates are worth a look. The Current solution line (6 of 6 against) is also missing from the screen with no note saying why.
screens.why_b5: No overclaim: the screen calls it 1 against and 1 asked, shows the single quote as *On their own (1)*, and keeps the 6 visible.
screens.why_b6: Chiara's answer adds two things I did not type: where a call center already covers after hours, missed calls stop being the pain. What takes its place is group requests and emails with no rates, and keeping rates right on every channel.

screens.why1: As the first screen it plainly checks whether I am the right person, an agent in a German hotel group's central reservations, before asking about my calls.
screens.why2: Reservation calls, hotel group and central reservations office are everyday words in my Munich office, and I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know without guessing whether I take booking calls through our central reservations office.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it completely for a gate, and a gate carries no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment, a hotel group in Germany with a central reservations office or call center, and nothing about a product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: One short question with two options is easy to hold; §17 would have it end simply *Yes or no.*, but it still says well.

screens.why1: Right after I said I take reservation calls at the central office, asking whether a booking call came in on my shift in the last week is nearly the same question again; of course one did, they come in all day.
screens.why2: Plain words for me, a booking call on my shift, I answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether calls came in on my shifts last week, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct, but No is true of no working agent, so in practice it is not a real choice.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is calls that go unanswered, after hours, at peak or on holidays; this gate asks only that a call came in, which drops the part that made it a problem.
screens.why6: Short, one question, said as 'Yes or no', easy to hold on the phone.
screens.why7: The gate asks the circumstance every agent is in, not the problem the founder counted, so every agent says Yes, nobody can say No, and the share can never refute the founder's band; this is the card's bad example.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call to your office go unanswered, on your shift or after it? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, a booking call came in on my shift this week, it is natural to ask how many days that happened.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are exactly how we talk in the reservations office, so I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know which days I worked last week, and on a trade-fair week every shift had booking calls, so I can answer from memory.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 plus I can't recall covers every true answer, and they don't overlap.
screens.why5: The problem is calls that don't get answered, but this asks only whether calls came in, which happens on every shift I work, so the founder's point has drifted to something ordinary.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold and answer.
screens.why7: Measure, shape and escape are as the card requires, but because a call comes in on every shift, my count just equals the shifts I worked (5 for me), so the options track my rota, not the problem, and can barely refute the belief.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on how many days did a caller hang up in the queue before anyone on your shift picked up? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking whether booking calls came in on my shifts and on how many days, it makes sense to ask which part of the work I'd most like made easier.
screens.why2: "Run of shifts on the phones," check-out rush, group requests and rates on every channel are all words we use in reservations, so I understand it on first reading.
screens.why3: I sit in the central reservations office in Munich, so the check-in and check-out rush and guests' requests at the desk are the front desk's work, not mine; I could only guess at those two.
screens.why4: Two of the five rows belong to the front desk rather than a central office, and the rates row is more revenue management than my own work, so the real choice for me is narrower than it looks.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks to me, but the founder's "Answering every booking call before it rings out" has become "Answering every call that comes in", which loses both "booking" and the moment before it rings out.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question with five short, parallel options and one escape at the end, easy to hold.
screens.why7: The own item is on the list, is not first, and "None of these" is at the first ask, but two rows are another role's setting (the front desk for a central office), and the own row has lost the founder's moment.
screens.instead: Think of your last run of shifts on the phones. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Answering every booking call before it rings out · Answering booking emails and group requests · Keeping rates right on every channel · Changing and cancelling existing bookings · Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After asking which part of the phones I'd most like made easier, asking how keeping up with the calls actually went is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: "Your last call" is one call, but "answering every call that comes in" is a whole shift, so I'd have to read it twice to work out whether you mean that one call or the shift around it.
screens.why3: I know how my last Saturday shift went with calls ringing out and callbacks, but one call can't have "a few rang out", so I'd guess you meant the shift.
screens.why4: The five cover what I see, from everything picked up to missed calls just gone, but they answer a shift and not the "last call" the stem names, and "few were called back" sits close to "simply lost".
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product reaches me; answering every call is just my job, and these are words we use in the reservations office.
screens.why6: Five options is holdable, but each of the middle three is two clauses said in one go (rang out, then called back), and that's a lot to keep straight when heard once.
screens.why7: There's a working first rung and an outright failure last, all on missed-and-recovered calls, but rungs two to four each join two states (how many rang out, and whether they were called back), and the stem's occasion (one call) doesn't match the act the rungs grade (a shift's calls).
screens.instead: Think of your last shift on the phones. How did keeping up with the calls go? Every call answered or called back quickly; a few missed, all called back that day; some missed, called back when there was time; many missed, few called back; or missed calls were simply lost. Or say someone else took the calls.
